title: Fact check: Every single part of this Trump story about South Korea is wrong
description: President Donald Trump told a story about South Korea on Monday. Every single part of it is false.
fullText:
President Donald Trump told a story about South Korea on Monday. Every single part of it is false.

Trump has delivered versions of his fictional story before; CNN debunked one telling last year. The president delivered Monday's version the day after he announced the US would reduce military exercises with South Korea – citing his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and also mentioning that South Korea declined to participate in the US war with Iran.

The latest version of Trump's tale, which you can watch in full here, went like this:

South Korea "essentially" didn't pay for the cost of the US military presence in the country before Trump first became president. Trump then got South Korea to unhappily agree to pay "$3 billion" in a year, with further increases the following year and the year after that. But then the 2020 election was "rigged" against him. When Joe Biden became president, South Korea convinced Biden that Trump was "probably a bad person" and they shouldn't have to pay the money, so Biden "immediately rescinded" Trump's "order."

Let's walk through why all of this is wrong. The facts show that Trump's comments include at least five separate inaccurate claims – in addition to his usual exaggeration of the size of the US military presence in South Korea, which he put at "39,000" but the Pentagon said was actually 26,589 as of the end of March.

Here's what Trump claimed Monday: "Just so you understand with South Korea, look: South Korea has been protected by us for many, many years, and during my first term, they agreed to pay close to $3 billion a year for protection, because we don't – you know, they essentially weren't paying." Last year, he explicitly said South Korea's cost-sharing payments didn't exist before he became president.

The reality: For decades before Trump took office, South Korea spent substantial sums to share the cost of the US military presence in the country; its cost-sharing "Special Measures Agreements" with the US began in 1991. Under the final five-year agreement signed before Trump became president in 2017, negotiated by the Obama administration, South Korea agreed to spend more than $800 million per year from 2014 through 2018. Trump is entitled to argue that this was insufficient, but it was far from not paying at all.

Here's what Trump claimed Monday: "But we agreed for a short term that it would be $3 billion…" Later in his remarks, he referred to the supposed arrangement as "$3 billion a year" from South Korea.

The reality: Under a one-year Special Measures Agreement negotiated by the Trump administration in 2019, South Korea agreed to an 8.2% increase in its spending – but the new total was still less than $1 billion, not $3 billion.

Here's what Trump claimed Monday: "But we agreed for a short term that it would be $3 billion, and next year it would go up and the next year it would go up, so that they start paying for their protection."

The reality: Trump did not secure three years of spending increases. He did achieve the one-year increase for 2019, but negotiations on a post-2019 deal stalled amid Trump's demands for a massive increase in South Korea's contribution, and the talks were still unresolved when Biden took office in January 2021.

South Korea did come to a narrower deal with the Trump administration in mid-2020 to spend $200 million that year to pay South Korean employees of US forces, who had been put on leave because Trump's one-year deal expired at the end of 2019. Clearly, though, that wasn't two years of spending hikes over the supposed "$3 billion."

Here's what Trump claimed Monday: "When the election was rigged and I ended up watching for four years and then coming back…"

The reality: Trump was lying. He lost the 2020 election fair and square to Biden.

Here's what Trump claimed Monday: "And South Korea, I get along with them very well. But they were paying $3 billion a year and then they convinced Biden that I was probably a bad person and they shouldn't. And he immediately rescinded that order."

The reality: Biden did not rescind any Trump cost-sharing agreement with South Korea. The only Special Measures Agreement signed by the Trump administration, the one-year 2019 deal, was dead by the time Biden took office in 2021 – and Biden's administration proceeded to sign two new agreements, one in 2021 and one in 2024, that both included South Korean spending increases.

The 2021 agreement – which retroactively covered Trump-era 2020 – included a South Korean spending increase of 13.9% in 2021, bringing the level to around $1 billion, then additional increases in 2022 through 2025 tied to increases in South Korea's defense budget. The 2024 agreement included an 8.3% increase in 2026 and then additional increases from 2027 to 2030 tied to South Korean inflation.

These were smaller hikes than Trump was demanding when he left office in early 2021. But, again, South Korea had not actually agreed to those Trump demands.

title: Opinion - No, the troops aren’t mentally weak. They just have terrible leadership.
description: Marine veteran Joslin Joseph criticizes the leadership of President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for prioritizing mission goals over troop welfare during an ongoing conflict with Iran.
fullText:
"Mission Accomplishment always comes before Troop Welfare." This mantra was drilled into me as a junior enlisted Marine and has stayed with me well into my career spanning professional sports, project management, and now as a writer. The premise is very simple. You always have to make sure that you focus on completing the mission. No matter if it's a life-or-death battle or something as pedestrian as a corporate product release.

You will have subordinates who always come up with plenty of needs, asks, excuses and problems that they need to deal with. They may have personal problems, financial issues, workplace conflicts, or just have lost motivation to work. And while you deal with all that, you must make sure that you are keeping an eye on the prize and getting you and your team to get the job done. This might make you the bad guy, but let's be honest. If you don't get the mission accomplished, you failed.

However, there is one major corollary to this mantra. Yes, mission accomplishment always comes before troop welfare. But if you aren't taking care of your troops, the chance of your mission succeeding drops substantially. Plenty of military leaders (and business leaders too) have always focused on the first part and completely ignored the second part to disastrous effects.

Enter the USS Abraham Lincoln. Reports of sailors and Marines tasked to the limit on a never ending deployment, plumbing issues, food shortages, and most damningly, being stuck in a combat zone for a war that we have won multiple times according to their commander-in-chief. If you were tuned into military circles, the rumors of terrible morale had abounded since a fire in the laundry room of another carrier, the USS Gerald Ford, broke out and forced that carrier into repairs.

But instead of coming home, President Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and what it's turning out to be a horde of yes-men in the Pentagon's upper civilian circle disregarded military leaders concerns of extended deployments, military readiness, manpower shortages, and the logistics of carrying out an offensive/naval blockade/missile defense/whatever Trump decides helps the stock market military operation against Iran.

Trump proving that he is not the military genius or beloved commander he makes himself out to be seemingly doubled down on the situation saying that their deployment wasn't long enough. Hegseth, a middle of the road military officer, has said that the pictures, news reports, and actual testimonies from the troops were misrepresented.

There is no doubt that the war with Iran that most Americans did not want is going poorly. But it takes a special type of incompetence to be the leader of a military and have a lack of awareness for how badly that affects morale.

Trump has long and rightfully been criticized for his lack of understanding of the sacrifice of military members. His disrespect for military awards, calling the war dead suckers and losers, and fudging the numbers of the war dead from the Iran conflict all stem from the fact that he views them as props.

When he needs a photo op, the troops are valuable to him. When he needs to give a State of the Union address and distract from the fact that the state of the union is terrible, he will march out soldiers and give them medals. A man who has mastered the art of social media deception learned that performative stunts like hugging flags, giving a thumbs up while standing on a grave in Arlington, or saluting a dead soldier in a Trump merch hat somehow convinces people that he actually cares.

But we are at war and the performance theatre of both Trump and Hegseth has gotten stale. We care about our troops being in harm's way and want them not just to be safe, but to be cared for. Military life isn't easy and no one is asking for these troops to be coddled. The troops themselves don't want to be coddled.

We will hear from the toxic vet-bro culture that these issues pale in comparison to what they did back in the day. We will get the veteran pissing contests that sound a lot like how your parents told you about how they walked to school. I have my own stories to tell. But I am also of the type of veteran to know that because I suffered, doesn't mean the people after me have to deal with stupid stuff too. Especially if it could be avoided.

Of course, we forget that Bob Hope didn't do USO Tours to look good for the public. It was because he knew how it affected soldiers to be away from home. There is a reason why mail delivery was important to locations as far away as Guadalcanal. There is a reason why we modernized our food preparation (thank you Chef Boyardee) to make sure troops were well fed. There is a reason why I got hundreds of letters from total strangers while I was in Iraq (I still have all of them).

Trump, Hegseth and their associates sold Americans on making the military more lethal. Instead, they started another forever war and stuck thousands of troops in the worst kind of stress with no support or relief. They forgot that taking care of troop welfare means a better chance of mission success. Or maybe they aren't good enough leaders to have known that in the first place.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary / Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

title: Who is Byron Donalds? The Trump ally is favored to become Florida's next governor.
description: It’s been over three decades since the Sunshine State elected a Democratic governor, but polls suggest the MAGA favorite could be in for a tight race in November.
fullText:
In February 2025, President Trump made a surprising endorsement in the Florida governor's race. It wasn't who he chose, but when he decided to back them that was unexpected. The primary was still 18 months away and the man he endorsed hadn't even declared his candidacy yet.

Still, Trump's word carries so much weight in the Republican Party, particularly in his newly adopted home state, that Rep. Byron Donalds quickly became the frontrunner in the Florida GOP gubernatorial primary.

"Byron Donalds would be a truly Great and Powerful Governor for Florida and, should he decide to run, will have my Complete and Total Endorsement," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time. "RUN, BYRON, RUN!"

Donalds formally entered the race five days after Trump's post. Throughout his campaign, polls have shown him well ahead of the other Republican candidates. If he wins the GOP primary on Tuesday, he would also be the favorite to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, who is ineligible to run for a third term.

It has been more than three decades since Florida elected a Democrat as its governor, but some of the GOP's victories during that span have been extremely close. Republicans are counting on Donalds to keep their winning streak alive as he gears up for what polls suggest could be another close contest against likely Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who left the GOP during Trump's first presidential term.

Here's a guide to who Byron Donalds is, what he stands for and what his potential election might mean for America's third most populous state.

Donalds, 47, was born in New York City in 1978. He is of Jamaican and Panamanian heritage and was raised by his mother, describing himself as the "product of a single-parent household." Donalds grew up in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn before moving to Florida for college. He graduated from Florida State University in 2002 with a bachelor's degree in finance and marketing, and stayed in Florida to launch a career in the banking and insurance industries.

Donalds has said that his inspiration to go into politics came from anger over how Congress handled the aftermath of the 2008 financial collapse and the ensuing bank bailouts. A registered Democrat at the time, Donalds opted to switch parties and embraced the fiscally conservative worldview of the burgeoning tea party movement, which advocated for low taxes and reduced government spending.

"I got mad," Donalds said during a podcast interview earlier this month. "It pissed me off. That's how I got into politics and from there got involved in the Tea Party."

As a young Black man, Donalds stood out within a movement that was largely associated with older white voters. In 2012, he joined a crowded GOP primary for an open House seat, but finished fifth out of six candidates. In 2016, he was elected to the Florida state legislature.

He ran for Congress again in 2020 and, after being labeled a "Rising Star" by Trump following his primary win, was elected to the House of Representatives for the first time. He was the third Black Republican in history to represent Florida on Capitol Hill.

When he joined Congress, Donalds was part of a group of conservative lawmakers called the "Freedom Force," who were dedicated to countering the influence of progressive lawmakers like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. One of his first acts after being sworn in was to challenge the certification of the 2020 presidential election. He has repeatedly said that he does not believe that Joe Biden was a legitimately elected president.

In 2023, his name was raised as a potential House speaker multiple times during a drawn-out leadership crisis that ultimately led to Rep. Mike Johnson being elected speaker.

Donalds has been married to his wife, Erika Lees, since 2003. They have three children together. According to Donalds's first wife, Bisa Hall, Donalds began dating Lees while he and Hall were still married. Hall told WGCU News their marriage was not romantic and that they only wed to resolve what she described as a "residency issue" affecting her ability to attend college in Florida.

In 2022, Donalds was captured on camera having a heated argument with a woman inside a supermarket in Naples, Fla. The woman, Kelly Mason, who is currently a member of the Collier County School Board, filed a civil lawsuit over the incident in July, accusing him of assault. In a statement, Donalds's campaign called the lawsuit "baseless" and "politically motivated."

Donalds has closely aligned himself with Trump's MAGA policies. The words "Enact the Trump Agenda" appear in large bold letters at the top of the "issues" page of his campaign website.

He has endorsed Trump's sweeping immigration crackdown, including arguing that undocumented immigrants facing deportation should not be entitled to due process under the law and criticizing the Supreme Court for striking down the president's attempt to revoke birthright citizenship.

Donalds is staunchly conservative on social issues. He supports placing strict limits on abortion access, wants to expand gun rights, has called for eliminating "woke ideology" in schools and supports restrictions on transgender rights, including barring transgender women and girls from women's sports. Donalds has also said he does not believe in man-made climate change.

If elected, he has pledged to block "sanctuary" jurisdictions that don't comply with federal immigration enforcement from receiving state funding, give parents more influence over their children's education and reform Florida's struggling property insurance industry.

The last time Florida elected a new governor with Trump in the White House was in the "blue wave" midterm cycle of 2018, when DeSantis narrowly defeated Democrat Andrew Gillum by less than half a percentage point. Though the national political environment appears to be swinging against the GOP again this year, polls have shown Donalds holding a steady lead of roughly five percentage points in head-to-head general election matchups.

title: Blanche: Trump administration may seek Supreme Court intervention in state voter rolls fight
description: Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Trump administration may look to the Supreme Court for help in a fight over state voter rolls. “Absolutely it’s a possibility. Election integrity is something th...
fullText:
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Trump administration may look to the Supreme Court for help in a fight over state voter rolls.

"Absolutely it's a possibility. Election integrity is something that President Trump ran on. And the American people elected him," Blanche told NBC News's Kristen Welker on "Meet the Press" in a Sunday interview when asked about taking the fight to the Supreme Court.

"It's something that every American should care about. And so the idea that the Department of Justice is trying to investigate issues around elections to make sure they're fair and make sure they're conducted the right way is not something that we should be running away from. That's something we should be running right towards," he added.

The Department of Justice has sued multiple states for not handing over sensitive, private voter data as requested. However, it has recently lost multiple cases in attempting to get that data.

Those moves come ahead of the 2026 midterms, which could be consequential for President Trump if Democrats win control of either or both chambers of Congress, which they appear poised to do.

Last month, Trump came forward with fresh accusations about the 2020 election, declassifying some documents while alleging U.S. elections were still insecure. Democrats quickly pushed back on the claims.

Trump, in a primetime address, said the intelligence community did not raise concerns as China accessed American voter rolls.

"Our purpose in disclosing this information is not to weaken confidence in elections, but to earn that confidence by confronting vulnerabilities and correcting them very, very quickly," Trump said from the White House.

title: Trump blames vandals for damaged grass in the spot where he held his big July 4 celebration
description: President Donald Trump says vandals are to blame for large swaths of dead grass on the National Mall near the World War II Memorial — in the spot where he had a stage built and hosted crowds for his J...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says vandals are to blame for large swaths of dead grass on the National Mall near the World War II Memorial — in the spot where he had a stage built and hosted crowds for his July 4 celebration.

Trump made the accusation in a social media post on Sunday without saying why he believes it's the work of vandals instead of trampled turf from the Independence Day festivities. The Republican president posted a photo showing a once-grassy area by the World War II Memorial, now patchy and brown across much of the sprawling turf.

"Look what VANDALS did to the grass connecting the vandalized World War II Monument and the vandalized Reflecting Pool, which will be opened again, and better than ever, shortly," Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

"Anybody who thinks the Reflecting Pool wasn't vandalized should go back to Law School!" he added.

Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals for damage to his renovation projects in the nation's capital, often without evidence and sometimes despite opposing accounts from his officials. Trump lashed out at U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro this month after her office concluded that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was the result of poor construction and not the work of vandals, as Trump claimed.

Authorities on Friday announced an arrest in connection with vandalism at the World War II Memorial, after the words "Clean hands dirty $" were found painted on the monument and bubbles filled a fountain. Pirro said felony charges were being brought against Melissa L. Farris, who was in custody and couldn't be reached for comment.

A woman identified on her Facebook page as Melissa Lovewell on Thursday posted a video in which she is seen taking cans of spray paint from her bag and then painting the monument. "I will wait here to be arrested for spraying our veterans' fountain," she says. "It was me. I'm doing it. It's on camera."

The woman was identified by her Kentucky driver's license as Melissa L. Farris, of Elizabethtown, Kentucky, an arrest warrant says.

Charging documents in that case make no mention of the grassy area Trump is highlighting in his new claims. Authorities said Farris had previously been arrested for camping on federal property a few blocks from the World War II Memorial, but not the area cited by Trump.

That stretch of lawn is instead where a large stage was built and crowds gathered to hear from Trump and watch fireworks at a July 4 event celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary. Trump claimed without providing evidence that more than 400,000 people attended the event before a storm hit the area and delayed his remarks.

On Aug. 1, Trump posted a different photo of the same area that appears to show the numbers "86 47" — which federal officials have said constitutes a threat against Trump, the 47th president — emblazoned into the grass. He cited it as evidence refuting Pirro's conclusion, calling it "a pure case of VANDALISM, that included the grass."

"There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!" he wrote.

Those numbers are not visible in the photo Trump posted to social media on Sunday.
